title: The Chain of Cards: a Lyon Weaver, the Pattern Taken Out of a Person, and the Statue Sold for Scrap Twice
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Couzon-au-Mont-d'Or, the branch called Jacquard
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources; placed at the birth year, the family's presence at Couzon being stated without dates
stops.campa: North of Lyon the Saone runs under limestone hills, and at Couzon-au-Mont-d'Or the Charles kindred quarry stone and barge it downriver to build the city. The grandfather is written into the records as Bartholomew Charles dit Jacquard: called Jacquard, the way a field gets called something. Pica Bourlemont's people came down the Rhone to this same junction with barges of cloth, watching the cargo turn from wool to silk. A house here, a vineyard and a quarry will come to Joseph, and he will sell all three to pay for a failure. The name is what he keeps.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
French Wikipedia, 'Couzon-au-Mont-d'Or' (limestone quarrying and the Saone stone trade)

stops.name: Saint-Maurice-de-Rotherens, the pattern-reader's village
stops.date_confidence: undated; the mother's origin is stated without a date and is carried only by the French article
stops.campa: East of the Rhone, in the hills of Savoie, lies the village of his mother. Antoinette Rive is a reader of woven patterns for the silk trade, which means she takes a design and works out, thread by thread, what the loom must be made to do. In 1752 this commune belongs to the Duchy of Savoy and not to the Kingdom of France; French troops arrive only in 1792, and it was Savoyard officers who arrested Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in this border country in 1488. The mother of the man France will decorate is, on the day he is born, a foreign subject who reads patterns for a living.
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'
French Wikipedia, 'Saint-Maurice-de-Rotherens' (Duchy of Savoy until the 1792 French occupation)

stops.name: Lyon, the birth in the silk trade
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A son is born in Lyon on the seventh of July, 1752, and registered as Joseph Marie Charles. The name the world will use is a nickname, Jacquard, borne by one branch of a large Charles kindred to keep it apart from the rest; he takes it formally later. The household works silk, and the sources will not agree whether the father is a master weaver at his own loom or a master manufacturer who owns the looms other men work. Twelve years earlier Jean-Jacques Rousseau had been tutoring the Mably children in this city. Nine children are born to the marriage; two grow up.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'

stops.name: Lyon, letters at thirteen
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the attested age; the sources give the age, not a date
stops.campa: His mother dies in 1762. He cannot read. Until he is thirteen he cannot read, and the reading is taught to him afterward, informally, by his brother-in-law Jean-Marie Barret, a printer and bookseller. Then he is apprenticed to a bookbinder. The boy who could not read is set to sewing and gluing the pages of books, holding text in order without being able to follow it. He had helped his father at the loom first; the work, says the one line the record gives, proved too arduous.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: Jean-Marie Barret, printer-bookseller of Lyon, brother-in-law and first teacher

stops.name: Lyon, the type foundry
stops.date_confidence: undated; placed between the bookbinding apprenticeship and the 1772 inheritance, the sources giving the trades in sequence without years
stops.campa: From binding he moves to casting: apprenticed to a maker of printers' type, standing over the mould where lead becomes a letter. Each sort is a separate object, interchangeable, kept in a case, set in a line to carry a message, then broken up and returned to the case. He learns this at the age when other Lyon boys learn the drawloom, where the pattern is carried instead by a child pulling cords in a fixed order, one cord at a time, all day, from memory or from a called-out list.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard' (the trades: relieur, type founder, quarry operator)
suggested_refs: The eighteenth-century Lyon drawloom and the tireur de lacs, the child who pulled the pattern cords

stops.name: Lyon, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in any source consulted
stops.campa: In 1772 the father dies and leaves his son the whole estate: the family house, the looms, the weaving workshop, a vineyard, and a stone quarry. Joseph is twenty. He is a weaver's son with property, which in Lyon is a different thing from being a weaver, and he sets about proving it by speculating in land. It goes badly. The trades he has learned, leather and lead and limestone, do not tell him how to hold an estate, and within a few years the inheritance is working against him.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: The 1772 inheritance: house, looms, workshop, vineyard, quarry

stops.name: Couzon-au-Mont-d'Or, the quarry and the vineyard
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the inheritance; the location of his quarry work is contradicted between sources and is not resolved here
stops.campa: The inherited quarry stands here above the Saone, where his grandfather's name was first written down as Jacquard. French accounts put his quarry-working years in the Bugey instead, a separate limestone country sixty kilometres east across the Rhone, and no source reconciles the two; both are recorded. Either way the trade is stone: cut, hauled, sold by weight. He comes to the loom by way of leather, lead and limestone, and no source consulted gives him a day of training in mechanics or names a master who taught him machines.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' (quarry at Couzon)
French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard' (quarry work in the Bugey)
suggested_refs: The unresolved Couzon-versus-Bugey question over where Jacquard worked stone

stops.name: Lyon, the marriage to Claudine Boichon
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of July, 1778, he marries Claudine Boichon, a Lyon widow of the middle class with property of her own and a dowry. The marriage record lists him as master weaver and silk merchant, which is what a man calls himself while he still owns looms. He will shortly not own them. A venture in figure-weaving, the patterned cloth that needs a drawloom and a child on the cords, fails, and takes him into debt deep enough to reach a courtroom.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' (marriage record, occupations, the failed figure-weaving venture)
suggested_refs: The 1778 marriage record naming him master weaver and silk merchant

stops.name: Oullins, the son and the house in her name
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested; the place is reconstruction, no source consulted stating where the birth occurred
stops.campa: Their only child, Jean Marie, is born on the nineteenth of April, 1779. The couple settle south of Lyon at Oullins, in a house held in Claudine's own name, which is why it survives the collapse that takes everything else. Brought to court, he sells the inheritance, the house at Couzon, the vineyard, the quarry, and uses his wife's dowry to settle what is still owing. He is a master weaver with no looms, living in a house he does not own, and the boy is an infant.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' (birth of the son; the court, the sale, the appropriated dowry; the Oullins house in Claudine's name)
suggested_refs: The Oullins house held in Claudine Boichon's name through the bankruptcy

stops.name: Bresse, the lime kilns
stops.date_confidence: undated; the 1911 Britannica reports the episode without a year, and it is placed here in the hardship between the bankruptcy and 1793
stops.campa: In the flat wet country of the Bresse he burns lime, feeding limestone into a kiln until it comes out caustic and white, work done by men with nothing else to do. In Lyon his wife plaits straw for money. Fifty years on, lecturing at the Conservatoire in Paris three years after Jacquard is dead, the economist Blanqui will describe the inventor as a plain straw-hat worker whose youth passed in the most obscure condition. No source names the kilns, or the years, or how long it lasted.
stops.quote: Jacquart etait un simple ouvrier en chapeaux de paille dont la jeunesse s'etait passee dans la condition la plus obscure.
stops.quote_source: Adolphe-Jerome Blanqui, Cours d'economie industrielle (1836-1837), dix-septieme lecon, delivered at the Conservatoire des arts et metiers; French Wikisource. The source spells the name Jacquart.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jacquard, Joseph Marie', via Wikisource
Adolphe-Jerome Blanqui, Cours d'economie industrielle, dix-septieme lecon, French Wikisource
suggested_refs: Blanqui's 1837 Conservatoire lecture, the earliest connected account of Jacquard read this session

stops.name: Lyon, the heights above the city: the siege
stops.date_confidence: the revolt and its suppression are attested to 1793; October is the month the siege ended, and no source places Jacquard at a named position
stops.campa: Lyon rises against the Convention and is besieged and beaten in the autumn of 1793. Jacquard and his son are in the city's defence, on the high ground where its fortifications traditionally run, the same slope that will later be built over with weavers' flats because his own loom needs tall frames. No source puts him at a named bastion. When the city falls he joins the revolutionary army that has just taken it, and takes the boy with him, and from here the record runs through a historian later judged unreliable.
sources: English Wikipedia and French Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' / 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: The 1793 siege of Lyon and the suppression of the city's revolt against the Convention

stops.name: Kehl, the Rhone-et-Loire battalion
stops.date_confidence: the campaign year is attested; the position is not, and the whole episode rests on Charles Ballot, whom English Wikipedia itself calls unreliable and rumour-repeating
stops.campa: Father and son enlist together in the Rhone-et-Loire battalion of the Army of the Rhine under Pichegru, and the campaign of 1795 works up and down the river through crossings like this one at Kehl, opposite Strasbourg. Nothing places Jacquard on this particular bank. The whole episode reaches the encyclopedias through the historian Charles Ballot, whom they themselves flag as a repeater of rumour. No second source names the battalion or puts him in it.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard', citing Charles Ballot
1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica via Wikisource
suggested_refs: Charles Ballot's account of Jacquard's military service, the sole authority and a distrusted one

stops.name: Near Heidelberg, the son shot down
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the year is attested, the day is not, and the account traces to Ballot, flagged as unreliable by later historians
stops.campa: Outside Heidelberg, in the fighting on the Rhine front, Jean Marie is killed. The tradition has him shot down at his father's side, sixteen years old, the only child of the marriage. Later historians flag the account and its source; the death itself is carried by both encyclopedias and by the 1911 Britannica. Jacquard goes back alone to a house at Oullins that stands in his wife's name, forty-three years old, with no son, no looms, and nothing of his father's estate left.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Rhine campaign of 1795 and the death of Jean Marie Jacquard

stops.name: Lyon, factory work and the spare hours
stops.date_confidence: undated; the 1911 Britannica places the return and the factory work in the later 1790s
stops.campa: He comes back to Lyon, takes work in a factory, and in the hours the work leaves him he thinks about looms. Everything before this is trades tried and money lost; everything after it is machines. The city he thinks in has woven silk for two centuries and been a hinge far longer: Clotilde was baptized at its cathedral of Saint-Jean, Athanasius Kircher passed through in 1638 carrying the loadstone and the hieroglyph. Its drawlooms need a second person, usually a child, to lift the right warp threads for every pass of the shuttle. The order exists, and it exists in a person.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica via Wikisource

stops.name: Lyon, the treadle loom
stops.date_confidence: year attested
stops.campa: In 1800 he builds an improved treadle loom, worked by the feet. It does not work well and finds no market, and it is the first of a run of devices that fail before the one that does not. He is forty-eight. Nobody in Lyon has any reason to connect the ruined speculator and lime-burner with the future of the trade, and the trade itself is at its lowest, the Revolution having ruined the luxury market that silk lives on. Nothing of the machine survives now except its year and the fact of its failure.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: Jacquard's 1800 treadle loom, the first of the failed inventions

segments.name: The Card Comes Out of the Loom

stops.name: Paris, the Cour carree du Louvre: a bronze medal
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the September dating of the an IX exposition is inferred, and the sources disagree over whether the machine shown here already selected by cards
stops.campa: He brings a loom to the industrial exposition of the year nine, held in the square courtyard of the Louvre among two hundred and twenty-nine exhibitors, and takes a bronze medal. Popular accounts move this exposition to the Champ de Mars four kilometres away, which had hosted the first edition in 1798; the courtyard is the right place. French sources say the machine here was already the card-controlled loom, others date that to the patent of 1804, and nothing consulted settles it.
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'
French Wikipedia, 'Exposition des produits de l'industrie francaise' (1801 in the Cour carree, 229 exhibitors)
suggested_refs: The Exposition des produits de l'industrie francaise of an IX, Cour carree du Louvre

stops.name: Lyon, a loom for fishing nets
stops.date_confidence: year attested
stops.campa: In 1803 he builds a machine for weaving fishing nets, a separate invention with its own fate: it does not sell either. A net is a grid of crossings, and at each crossing a knot either exists or does not, so the machine has to be told, crossing by crossing, which. He is working the same problem from a second direction without any source remarking on it, and it is the net loom, not the silk loom, that first turns the government's attention onto him.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: Jacquard's 1803 net-weaving loom

stops.name: Paris, the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month given
stops.campa: Summoned to Paris in 1803, he is attached to the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers, the state's warehouse of machines, and given the means to develop his invention. In its stores stands a loom built half a century earlier by Jacques de Vaucanson, maker of the flute-playing automaton and the digesting duck, who had tried to automate the drawloom and failed to interest anybody in it. The machine has been sitting in a room in Paris waiting for a bookbinder from Lyon to walk past.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: The Vaucanson loom in the collections of the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers

stops.name: Paris, Vaucanson's loom taken apart in the mind
stops.date_confidence: the year of the study is inferred from the English article's sequence; only the 1804 patent is firmly dated
stops.campa: Urged on by the fabric maker Gabriel Dutillieu, he studies the stored Vaucanson loom closely. Behind it stand two more men: Basile Bouchon, who in 1725 ran a punched paper tape through a loom, and Jean-Baptiste Falcon, who in 1728 replaced the tape with a chain of stiff cards laced edge to edge. Vaucanson's own automated looms are dated between 1745 and 1755 by the French sources and to 1740 by the English, a discrepancy nobody has closed. Jacquard invents none of these parts. He assembles them.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' and 'Jacquard machine' (Bouchon 1725, Falcon 1728, Vaucanson)
French Wikipedia, 'Jacques de Vaucanson' and 'Metier Jacquard' (looms dated 1745-1755, 'as early as 1745')
suggested_refs: Bouchon's 1725 punched paper tape and Falcon's 1728 chain of cards, the two mechanisms Jacquard combined

stops.name: Paris, the patent
stops.date_confidence: the patent year is attested; French sources date the card-controlled loom itself to 1801, and the conflict is left open
stops.campa: The refined card-controlled mechanism is patented in 1804. What it does is small and total: a chain of pasteboard cards passes over a prism, and where a card has a hole a needle passes through and lifts a hook, and where it has no hole the needle is blocked and the hook stays down. The pattern stops being something a person remembers and becomes something an object holds. Five years later he will write of the machine himself, in the register of a man selling a tool.
stops.quote: The machine that I created is simple, costs virtually nothing to maintain, and only requires being kept clean, protected from rust and dust. … This is not all: the fabric is created with speed and perfection, the designs go with the warp of the thread, and the outlines are imperceptible and blended, like in painting.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Joseph Jacquard, 'Notice on the inventions and improvements introduced in the industry of Lyon by Joseph Jacquard since January 1, 1809 until today' (1809), as quoted in English Wikiquote; the French original was not located this session, and the internal ellipsis is present in the source as quoted
sources: Timeline summary of the Jacquard machine drawing on Wikipedia, 'Jacquard machine'
English Wikiquote, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' (the 1809 Notice)
suggested_refs: The 1809 Notice sur les inventions et perfectionnements, unlocated in French this session

stops.name: Paris, the paper strip abandoned for the chain of cards
stops.date_confidence: the English article places the change 'by 1805' without a month; it sits after the 1804 patent date in the same source, an ordering the sources do not explain
stops.campa: He has been working with a strip of paper, and by 1805 he gives it up and goes back to Falcon's chain of separate cards laced together. The reason is mechanical and it is the whole invention: a strip is one object, so altering any part of a pattern means making a new strip, while a chain of cards can be lengthened, repaired card by card, lifted out and stored and put back. Guaman Poma de Ayala drew Andean officials holding quipus, whole records kept in knotted cord; keeping a pattern outside a person is older than the loom that will make it famous.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard'

segments.name: The Emperor, the City, the Prud'hommes

stops.name: Lyon, the Emperor and the Empress at the loom
stops.date_confidence: attested by both encyclopedias; the building of the demonstration is not identified in any source
stops.campa: On the twelfth of April, 1805, travelling south toward his coronation as King of Italy, Napoleon comes to Lyon with Josephine and is shown the loom. Blanqui, thirty years later, reports the Emperor's greeting: so it is you who wrestle with God, and claim to make knots on a taut rope. The sentence is printed in an 1837 lecture and nowhere earlier, so the words are verified and the occasion of them is not. Jacquard is fifty-two, and has spent most of his adult life in debt or in the army.
stops.quote: C'est donc vous qui luttez avec le bon Dieu, et prétendez faire des nœuds sur une corde tendue ?
stops.quote_source: Words attributed to Napoleon addressing Jacquard, as reported in Adolphe-Jerome Blanqui, Cours d'economie industrielle (1836-1837), dix-septieme lecon, French Wikisource. The sentence is verified as printed; the attribution itself is unconfirmed beyond this retelling.
sources: English Wikipedia and French Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' / 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'
Adolphe-Jerome Blanqui, Cours d'economie industrielle, dix-septieme lecon, French Wikisource
suggested_refs: Napoleon's visit to Lyon, 12 April 1805, on the journey to the Italian coronation

stops.name: Lyon, the patent given to the city
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested; the place is inferred, since no source says where the act was signed and the Emperor was in Lyon three days before
stops.campa: Three days after the visit the loom's patent is granted to the city of Lyon, and Jacquard is given a state pension of three thousand francs for life and a royalty of fifty francs on every machine built to his design, running from 1805 to 1811. The invention is taken off him and paid for in the same act. Joseph Fourier will hold the prefecture of this same Rhone department for a few weeks in 1815, and had held the Isere at Grenoble for thirteen years: one administrative machine, buying a loom here and a mathematician there.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' (patent to the city; pension of 3,000 francs; 50-franc royalty 1805-1811)

suggested_refs: The imperial act of 15 April 1805 assigning the loom's patent to the city of Lyon

stops.name: Lyon, the Academy's prize
stops.date_confidence: traditional: carried by the French article alone and not corroborated by any other source consulted
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of August the Academy of Lyon, the city's society of sciences, letters and arts, awards him an inventor's prize. Only the French encyclopedia carries this, and nothing else consulted repeats it. Lyon's learned men honour the machine in August; Lyon's weavers are already against it. The city will spend the next decade holding both positions at once, decorating the invention in one building and refusing to install it in the next street.
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: The prize records of the Academie des sciences, belles-lettres et arts de Lyon for 1805

stops.name: Paris, declared public property
stops.date_confidence: the 1911 Britannica dates the public-property declaration to 1806; a compressed retelling folds it into 15 April 1805, and the two are deliberately kept apart here
stops.campa: In 1806 the government declares the loom public property, so that any manufacturer may build it. The figure of eleven thousand machines in use by 1812 is repeated everywhere and disputed by historians, and real growth in sales comes only after 1815. A machine can be declared public and still not be installed. What the mechanism still wants is Jean-Antoine Breton, who will correct the card selection before the trade will take it. Any manufacturer may now build the loom without paying its inventor a franc. Jacquard keeps the pension until 1811, and the name.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica via Wikisource (public property, 1806)
English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' (the disputed 11,000 figure; growth after Breton's fix)
suggested_refs: The 1806 declaration of the loom as public property, and the disputed count of 11,000 looms by 1812

stops.name: Lyon, the loom broken in the public square
stops.date_confidence: undated and unresolved. No source consulted gives a year, an agent, or a place for the destruction; accounts spread it anywhere between 1801 and 1812, and this date is a placeholder inside that window, not a claim
stops.campa: The most retold event of his life has no date. The English article mentions in passing that an exhibit loom of his was destroyed and names nobody. Blanqui, closest to it in 1837, says they wanted to stone him, and that his loom was broken in the public square by order of the prud'hommes, the guild court, the wood and the iron sold off as scrap. That is not a mob: it is a judgement, with an auction afterward. The story that the pieces went into the Rhone appears in no source read here.
stops.quote: on voulut le lapider, et son métier fut brisé en place publique par ordre des prud'hommes ; le bois et le fer qui le composaient furent vendus comme matériaux de rebut
stops.quote_source: Adolphe-Jerome Blanqui, Cours d'economie industrielle (1836-1837), dix-septieme lecon, French Wikisource
sources: Adolphe-Jerome Blanqui, Cours d'economie industrielle, dix-septieme lecon, French Wikisource

French Wikipedia, 'Metier Jacquard' (machine-breaking by canuts, no year)

stops.name: Lyon, Breton's hands on the mechanism
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1806 and again for 1817; both improvements are carried in this one stop, and the English article credits the commercially decisive fix to Breton after 1815
stops.campa: The mechanism that carries one man's name begins to sell only once a second man has repaired it. Jean-Antoine Breton improves it in 1806 and improves it again in 1817, and it is his correction of the card selection that the trade finally accepts. Blanqui gives the reason Lyon changed its mind, and it is not admiration. Only later, when foreign competition began to be felt and to become formidable, did the ungrateful Lyonnais come back from their unjust prejudice and adopt at last the loom invented by their able compatriot.
stops.quote: Ce ne fut que plus tard, et lorsque la concurrence étrangère commença à se faire sentir et à devenir redoutable, que les ingrats Lyonnais revinrent de leur injuste prévention, et adoptèrent enfin le métier inventé par leur habile compatriote
stops.quote_source: Adolphe-Jerome Blanqui, Cours d'economie industrielle (1836-1837), dix-septieme lecon, French Wikisource
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard' (Breton's improvements of 1806 and 1817)
English Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' (growth in sales after Breton's post-1815 fix)

stops.name: Paris, Knight of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: attested by the French article; the ceremony's place is not stated and the pin is the canonical Paris point
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of November, 1819, under a restored monarchy with no reason to love anything Napoleon paid for, he is made a Knight of the Legion of Honour. He is sixty-seven. The pension ran out eight years earlier and the royalty with it, and the looms multiplying across Lyon and then across Europe owe him nothing at all, the patent having belonged to the city since 1805 and to anybody who wanted it since 1806. The Bourbon state decorates him for a machine the Empire bought from him and then handed to anyone who asked.
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'
suggested_refs: The Legion of Honour register entry of 17 November 1819

stops.name: Oullins, the town hall
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month given
stops.campa: In 1826 the town that has housed him since the year his son was born makes him a municipal councilor. He is seventy-four, retired at Oullins on the Rhone side of Lyon, in the house that stood in Claudine's name. The office is small and local, the kind of honour a village gives a man it has watched for fifty years, and it is the only public position he ever holds. Gilles Deleuze will hold a fellowship and then a teaching post a few kilometres up the same river.
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'

stops.name: Lyon, the canuts come down the hill
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by the French article; no month or day is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In 1831 Lyon's silk weavers rise. They are called canuts, and they work Jacquard-type looms in high-ceilinged flats on the Croix-Rousse slope, flats built tall because his frames are tall; the whole quarter is a consequence of the machine. Their protest names automation as the cause of unemployment. Half a century later William Morris will set hand looms working at Merton Abbey against the factory loom, and a century after that Anni Albers will write On Weaving with the same argument still open.
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard' (the 1831 canut uprising and the association of the looms with unemployment)

stops.name: Oullins, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested by both encyclopedias
stops.campa: He dies at Oullins on the seventh of August, 1834, aged eighty-two, in a house that never belonged to him. He has outlived his wife's dowry, his father's estate, his son, his patent and his pension. The machine that carries his name is by then standard equipment in the trade that broke one of his looms in a public square, and it is being built by manufacturers who owe him no royalty because a government declared it public property twenty-eight years before.
sources: English Wikipedia and French Wikipedia, 'Joseph Marie Jacquard' / 'Joseph-Marie Jacquard'

stops.name: Cimetiere d'Oullins, the grave
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the burial is carried by the French article alone, the date defaults to the day of death, and the pin is approximate, two coordinate pairs about 460 m apart circulating for the grave
stops.campa: He is buried in the cemetery of Oullins. The French encyclopedia says the tomb is still visible; no source consulted gives the plot, and no cemetery register was read for this journey. The English article says nothing about a burial at all. For a man whose invention exists precisely in order to record a position exactly, the position of his own body is recorded twice, differently, and neither record can be checked against the other. The cemetery lies a few streets from the house, and the town has grown around both.

stops.name: Lyon, the portrait woven in silk
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month given, and the commissioning firm is a gap
stops.campa: Five years after his death a portrait of Jacquard is woven in silk on one of his own looms, using something like twenty-four thousand punched cards: the man seated in a coat beside a small model loom, rendered by the process he assembled. It is called the most famous image in the early history of computing. The commissioning firm is usually given as Didier Petit et Cie, an attribution the pages fetched for this journey do not carry, so it stands here as a gap and not a fact.
stops.quote: It is known as a fact that the Jacquard loom is capable of weaving any design which the imagination of man may conceive.
stops.quote_source: Charles Babbage, Passages from the Life of a Philosopher, Chapter VIII (London, 1864)

stops.name: London, algebraical patterns
stops.date_confidence: the publication year of the note is attested; the pin is placed with the portrait rather than at any address of Lovelace's
stops.campa: Ada Lovelace, translating Menabrea's sketch of the Analytical Engine and adding notes longer than the paper itself, writes that the engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves. Babbage in the same decade writes that his engine can be understood by anyone acquainted with the principles of the loom. The comparison is not decoration: both of them are describing one mechanism, a chain of holes that tells a machine what to do next.
stops.quote: We may say most aptly, that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves.
stops.quote_source: Ada Lovelace, Note A to L. F. Menabrea, 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine Invented by Charles Babbage, Esq.', Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 (1843); text confirmed via the fourmilab reproduction and the Wikisource listing

stops.name: London, the sheet mistaken for an engraving
stops.date_confidence: the anecdote is undated in Babbage's text; 1864 is the publication year of Passages, and the pin is the modern Science Museum, which holds a copy of the portrait, not a period address
stops.campa: A copy of the woven silk reaches Charles Babbage, who keeps it framed and glazed and shows it to visitors, Prince Albert among them, and records that two members of the Royal Academy took it for an engraving. Cloth pretending to be a print, made by a machine reading holes. He is at that time trying to build an engine that will do arithmetic from instructions held outside itself, and he takes the cards from the loom because the loom has already solved the problem he is stuck on.
stops.quote: The portrait of Jacquard was, in fact, a sheet of woven silk, framed and glazed, but looking so perfectly like an engraving, that it had been mistaken for such by two members of the Royal Academy.
stops.quote_source: Charles Babbage, Passages from the Life of a Philosopher, Chapter XI (London, 1864)

stops.name: Lyon, the prayer book of silk
stops.date_confidence: produced 1886-1887; the card count is reported anywhere from 106,000 to 500,000 depending on the source, and the spread is not resolved
stops.campa: The Livre de Prieres is woven on Jacquard-descended looms in 1886 and 1887, a book of prayers made entirely of silk, letters and borders and all. The number of cards it took is given as a hundred and six thousand by one source and five hundred thousand by another, and that spread is itself the finding. Anni Albers, whose On Weaving sets Bauhaus structural diagrams beside pre-Columbian cloth, traces the drawloom, the Jacquard attachment and the power loom as one lineage.

stops.name: Washington, the census in holes
stops.date_confidence: the census year is attested; the pin is the federal capital, no specific building being named in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Herman Hollerith adapts the punched card to the United States census of 1890, and a person becomes a row of holes to be counted by machine. The industry that grows out of it becomes IBM. Babbage had already described the arrangement exactly, in the loom's own terms, a quarter of a century before there was a census machine to describe. Half a century after him the pattern being punched is a population, and the artist who designed it is a bureau. The object is unchanged: stiff, rectangular, punched, read by needles feeling for holes.
stops.quote: by means of a certain machine, punches holes in a set of pasteboard cards in such a manner that when those cards are placed in a Jacquard loom, it will then weave upon its produce the exact pattern designed by the artist
stops.quote_source: Charles Babbage, Passages from the Life of a Philosopher, Chapter VIII (London, 1864)

stops.name: Milan, the cards give way to electricity
stops.date_confidence: year and exhibition attested
stops.campa: At the textile machinery exhibition in Milan in 1983, Bonas Textile Machinery shows the first successful electronic Jacquard machine, and the chain of pasteboard gives way to a signal. The cards last a hundred and seventy-nine years from the patent. By then their descendants have run through Hollerith's census, the punched cards and the implosion calculations that Tony Skyrme's journey records at Los Alamos, John von Neumann's machines, and Claude Shannon's programme for a computer playing chess.

stops.name: Lyon, place Sathonay: the bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested by the French article for both date and site
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of August, 1840, six years after his death, Lyon inaugurates a bronze statue of Jacquard by Denis Foyatier on place Sathonay, honouring him as a benefactor of the city's workers. English sources add that the site is where an exhibit loom of his had been destroyed; the French account of the inauguration says nothing of the kind, and since no source dates the destruction the claim cannot be tested. The city casts in metal what it once sold as scrap metal.

stops.name: Lyon, place de la Croix-Rousse: the statue moves uphill
stops.date_confidence: the subject article says the statue was moved in 1898; the article on the square says the Foyatier bronze there was inaugurated in 1901. Both are recorded and neither is preferred
stops.campa: The statue is carried up to the place de la Croix-Rousse, into the weavers' quarter the loom itself created, so that the figure stands among flats built tall to hold his frames. The two French articles disagree by three years about when this happens, one saying moved in 1898 and the other inaugurated in 1901. This is the square where the canuts of 1831 gathered, and where by now their grandchildren work the machine their grandfathers went into the street against.

stops.name: Calais, the monument in a lace town
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not given
stops.campa: Calais raises a monument to Jacquard in 1907, sculpted by Marius Roussel. Calais is a lace town rather than a silk town, and the sources name only the monument and its sculptor, never the reason a Channel port four hundred kilometres from Lyon should want a statue of a Lyon weaver. That the card mechanism had by then been fitted to looms making cloth other than silk is the likeliest answer, and it is not one any source consulted actually gives. Lace is a cloth that is mostly holes, patterned by a machine that reads holes.

stops.name: Saint-Etienne, place Jacquard
stops.date_confidence: executed 1911-1912, inaugurated 1912, listed as a historic monument in 2016
stops.campa: Saint-Etienne, the ribbon-weaving city southwest of Lyon, has a square called place Jacquard, and between 1911 and 1912 the sculptor Paul Landowski makes a monument to stand in it. It is inaugurated in 1912 and listed as a historic monument in 2016. Ribbon is narrow cloth and its patterns are small and endlessly repeated, exactly the work a chain of cards does without tiring, and this town's looms are still running on his mechanism long after the trade that refused it is gone.

stops.name: Paris, the stamp
stops.date_confidence: year attested, marking the centenary of the death; no issue date given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In 1934, the centenary of his death, the French postal service issues a stamp with his face on it. A stamp is a small standard object, perforated at its edges so it can be separated from its neighbours, sold in sheets and cancelled by machine. A hundred and thirty years after the patent, the state that took his invention and made it public property is circulating his portrait as a perforated unit of paper, priced, gummed and repeated by the sheet.

stops.name: Lyon, place de la Croix-Rousse: melted, then cut in stone
stops.date_confidence: the melting in 1942 and the stone replacement of 1947 are both attested; the two events are carried in this one stop
stops.campa: In 1942, under Vichy, the bronze is taken down and melted as part of the mobilization of metal, the second time a statue or a machine of his is broken up and sold for the material in it. In 1947 Elie Ottavry cuts a replacement in stone and it is set on the same site, where it stands now. The first breaking was ordered by a guild court and the second by a collaborating government, and both times the metal was worth more than the likeness. Foyatier's bronze had stood a hundred and two years, in two squares, before it went to the furnace.

stops.name: Roubaix, the bust in the swimming pool
stops.date_confidence: undated: the sources name the bust and its sculptor but give no year. The date field is a placeholder chosen to sort last in the sequence and asserts nothing
stops.campa: At Roubaix in the far north, a municipal swimming pool built between the wars is now the Musee d'art et d'industrie Andre-Diligent, and among its holdings is a bust of Jacquard by the sculptor C.M. Iguel. A northern weaving town keeps his likeness in a converted bath house, under a name that couples art to industry. No source consulted dates the bust or says when it entered the collection. He is in street names at Nancy, Paris and Reims, and in two lycees, at Caudry and at Oullins, where he died.
